repairs.defensible_basis: The creator formula at 45:18 begins a fresh declaration after the nations' submission speech, and the summons to the ends of the earth develops into the court confession at 45:23-25. Later reuse of the knee-and-tongue language does not interrupt Isaiah's own closing cadence.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 45:18-25 as a creator declaration joined to a judicial appeal. Ending at 45:25 keeps the every-knee climax and Israel-offspring epilogue together; a citation-based subdivision would import a seam from outside the passage.

primary_reviews.support: The Hebrew ki-koh-amar construction at 45:18 restarts direct divine speech, while the oath sequence reaches its grammatical completion in verses 23-25.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 14 already began a nations-response panel, so 18 can also be read as an internal intensification within 45:14-25.

primary_reviews.support: A creator self-identification, courtroom summons, universal invitation, oath, and final vindication statement form one escalating appeal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The speech contains several imperatives that could tempt smaller excerpts, especially the turn at verse 22.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical reuse of the appeal and oath identifies important relations but supplies no independent evidence for an internal Isaiah boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The remembered wording can bias reviewers toward famous-verse extraction even when the local address continues.

repairs.defensible_basis: Bel and Nebo fall at the opening, after which carried idols are contrasted repeatedly with a people borne from birth; manufacture and failed petition finish the satire in verse 7. Extending through verse 13 would swallow the new command to remember.
repairs.boss_rationale: Retain 46:1-7 as the first half of the chapter's idol disputation. The immobile image that cannot answer is the proper terminus, whereas a chapter-wide chunk would hide the imperative and purpose speech beginning at 46:8.

primary_reviews.support: The named subjects Bel and Nebo establish the opening tableau, and the carried-versus-carrying verbal contrast runs through the unanswering idol in 46:7.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Masoretic paragraphing alone cannot prove that the satire is independently retrievable from the chapter's following address.

primary_reviews.support: The humiliation, loading, carrying, manufacture, and unanswered cry constitute a complete mock-procession satire.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The remembrance speech in 46:8-13 answers the same idol problem and therefore remains a strong sibling under the chapter parent.

primary_reviews.support: Babylon and idol parallels elsewhere illuminate the imagery, but they do not determine whether Isaiah 46 should be exposed at one or two levels.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A reader may need the succeeding promise of near salvation to understand the satire's argumentative purpose.

repairs.defensible_basis: The doubled remembrance command at 46:8 turns from the idol tableau to a direct argument about former acts, declared purpose, and approaching salvation. Zion and glory supply the endpoint in verse 13, so neither agent chronology nor chapter convenience governs the span.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 46:8-13 as a remembrance-and-purpose address. It begins with a new audience imperative and ends with the promised location of salvation; merging 1-13 would obscure this answer, while extracting the eastern agent would invite chronological overreach.

primary_reviews.support: Zikhru-zot at 46:8 is a new plural imperative, and the first-person purpose declarations resolve with salvation-in-Zion at 46:13.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The speech remains semantically linked to the idols of verses 1-7, making the whole chapter a necessary hydration parent.

primary_reviews.support: Remember, recall, listen, and the near-salvation announcement produce a coherent disputation-response rather than a miscellaneous promise list.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The agent-from-the-east statement in verse 11 has enough prominence to attract an unwarranted isolated unit.

primary_reviews.support: No canonical parallel fixes the internal break at 46:8; the decision rests on Isaiah's direct imperative and argumentative turn.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later interpretations of the agent could distort the boundary into a ruling about identity or date.

repairs.defensible_basis: The command to descend and sit in dust launches a sustained daughter-Babylon taunt; verse 8 sharpens the accusation but retains the same female addressee until astrologers, traders, and the final absence of a savior close the poem. The taunt therefore survives its internal escalation.
repairs.boss_rationale: Keep 47:1-15 whole and accepted. The renewed 'hear now' at verse 8 is a real strophic hinge, yet it does not replace the governing address begun in verse 1; splitting there would detach the failed-expert verdict from the dethronement it answers.

primary_reviews.support: Second-feminine imperatives and accusations sustain the daughter-city address from the dust command through the no-savior conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The discourse marker at 47:8 is substantial and could support literary children even though the Hebrew addressee continues.

primary_reviews.support: The literary primary treats 47:1-7 as dethronement and 47:8-15 as a complacency indictment with an expert catalogue.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Preserving one taunt better retains the reversal from claimed permanence to abandoned specialists.

challenge.claim: Verse 47:8 may open a separately retrievable accusatory stanza.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Test 47:1-7 and 47:8-15 as children with compulsory 47:1-15 hydration.

primary_reviews.support: Later Babylon taunts may echo this poem, but those relations cannot decide whether verse 8 is an active seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Reception history creates a risk of reading later city imagery back into Isaiah's unit structure.

repairs.defensible_basis: The 'hear this, house of Jacob' summons opens a long accusation about false naming, foretelling, obstinacy, and refining. The repeated 'for my sake' rationale in verse 11 completes that defense before a second listen command changes the speech at verse 12.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 48:1-11 as the indictment-and-refinement movement. Its final concern is the divine name and glory, not the speaker puzzle of verse 16; treating all of chapter 48 as one chunk would bury the explicit readdress at 48:12.

primary_reviews.support: The initial shim'u-zot governs accusations and first-person explanations through the doubled self-sake statement of verse 11.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal paragraph marks and changes from accusation to disclosure occur within 1-11, but none supplies a stronger close than verse 11.

primary_reviews.support: An addressed indictment moves from hypocritical naming through prior prediction to the refining explanation, then ends on withheld glory.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 6-8 introduce 'new things' and could be overread as a separate oracle rather than an internal evidentiary panel.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical discussions of foreknowledge and refining do not furnish an independent literary seam for Isaiah 48.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The chapter's later departure command is relevant context and must remain linked through the 46-48 parent.

repairs.defensible_basis: The renewed 'listen to me, Jacob and Israel' at verse 12 starts a creator-and-agent address, but verse 16 ends with a difficult first-person claim about being sent. That syntactic pressure is preserved inside this medium-confidence unit rather than resolved by naming the speaker.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 48:12-16 provisionally as the complete listen-and-sent-speaker movement. The next verse begins a clear redeemer formula, whereas splitting verse 16 to force an identity solution would make the chunk map perform exegesis it is not authorized to decide.

primary_reviews.support: The plural approach-and-hear imperatives in 48:16 and the clause 'now the Lord YHWH has sent me' introduce a real speaker-assignment difficulty.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The fresh listen command at 48:12 and redeemer formula at 48:17 still provide defensible outer bounds.

challenge.claim: The discourse identity and attachment of the final clause in 48:16 remain unresolved.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain 48:12-16 at medium confidence and obtain direct Hebrew discourse review before any smaller child is surfaced.

primary_reviews.support: Creator assertions, the chosen agent, the call to draw near, and the sent-speaker statement make a compact but deliberately ambiguous address.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 16 contains an internal turn that a clause-level model could represent more precisely than the present verse-granular route.

primary_reviews.support: Other canonical speaker and sending texts cannot identify the voice here or manufacture a boundary inside verse 16.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-references may increase interpretive pressure precisely where the local syntax remains unsettled.

repairs.defensible_basis: The redeemer-and-Holy-One formula at 48:17 changes the mode to teaching, lament over missed obedience, and an imperative departure from Babylon. The exodus-like report culminates in the no-peace refrain at verse 22, which closes the chapter's final movement.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 48:17-22 as a teaching and departure oracle. Verse 20 belongs with the command, announced proclamation, and water-from-rock sequence; isolating the famous exit line would strip away both its introduction and its no-peace coda.

primary_reviews.support: A new koh-amar formula names redeemer and teacher at 48:17, while the exodus imperatives and no-peace saying carry the speech to verse 22.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 20 is marked by plural imperatives and can function as an internal proclamation panel.

primary_reviews.support: Instruction, counterfactual lament, departure summons, travel provision, and refrain make one deliberately varied closing oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The no-peace line could be treated as a floating refrain, but here it functions as the chapter's explicit coda.

primary_reviews.support: Exodus relations illuminate the departure imagery without independently selecting verse 20 or 22 as a retrieval seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Extracting the Babylon command through later reuse could hide the preceding teacher-and-way frame.

repairs.defensible_basis: The coastlands imperative opens a first-person call testimony: womb naming, weapon images, reported commission, lament, and an enlarged mission. Verse 6 finishes that commissioning dialogue at the end of the earth before a new divine formula addresses the despised figure.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 49:1-6 as a servant-call and mission unit without deciding who the speaker is. The formal response at verse 7 creates the next seam; an identity-based split inside 1-6 would confuse a contested referent with observable literary form.

primary_reviews.support: Plural coastlands commands, first-person perfects, embedded divine speech, and the culminating mission infinitive form a complete testimony.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The referent of 'Israel' in verse 3 and the return language in verses 5-6 remain translation and identity hot zones.

primary_reviews.support: Call report, vocational imagery, complaint, answer, and expanded commission trace a recognizable prophetic testimony arc.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The internal speech shifts at verses 3 and 5 are real but remain parts of one recounted commissioning event.

primary_reviews.support: Later quotations of the light-to-nations line demonstrate relation, not an Isaiah seam or an identity verdict.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Famous-line retrieval could sever verse 6 from the failure-and-answer sequence that gives it literary force.

repairs.defensible_basis: The redeemer formula at verse 7 begins a response promising recognition, restoration, release, provision, and return; heaven, earth, and mountains answer with praise in verse 13. That hymnic close completes the response rather than merely decorating it.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 49:7-13 as the response to the preceding call testimony. Keeping the cosmic praise with the promise prevents a split between announced restoration and its formal acclamation, while the Zion complaint at verse 14 unmistakably opens another voice.

primary_reviews.support: Koh-amar at 49:7 resets the address, and the imperative cosmic praise at verse 13 marks a completed response before 'Zion said.'
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Several promise panels have paragraph-level interest, but no internal formula displaces the full response-and-hymn frame.

primary_reviews.support: Royal recognition, covenant restoration, prisoner release, pastoral provision, gathering, and creation praise rise as one answer sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 8-12 could be indexed as promise subpanels only if their dependence on the response formula remains explicit.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical reuse of individual restoration lines cannot determine whether the poem should be subdivided for retrieval.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The 49:1-13 macro-parent remains important because the response presupposes the servant testimony.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'Zion said' gives verse 14 a new speaker and complaint; the answer uses maternal memory, engraved walls, returning children, and a series of astonished questions. The final 'who has brought up these?' question at verse 21 completes the abandoned-to-overfull reversal.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 49:14-21 as Zion's complaint and maternal-children answer. Verse 22 introduces a fresh divine formula and a nations-standard scene, so merging that panel would mute the carefully staged movement from private lament to astonished recognition.

primary_reviews.support: The reporting clause 'Zion said' opens a complaint-answer exchange, and the interrogatives of verses 20-21 finish its child-count tableau.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The answer continues thematically into the nations' return of children in verses 22-23.

primary_reviews.support: A single voiced complaint is answered through maternal comparison and the visible arrival of children, ending in astonishment rather than decree.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The boundary is relationally porous because the next unit explains how those children are carried back.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem warns that 49:14-50:3 may require strong hydration across Zion, children, captors, and the divorce-creditor disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The explicit voice and formula changes still justify local children under that cross-chapter parent.

challenge.claim: Independent retrieval of 49:14-21 may weaken the argument continuing through 50:3.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Require 49:14-50:3 hydration whenever this complaint-answer child is surfaced.

repairs.defensible_basis: A new 'thus says the Lord YHWH' at verse 22 raises a signal to nations, depicts children carried home, and answers whether captives can be taken from the mighty. The all-flesh recognition formula at verse 26 supplies a categorical close.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 49:22-26 as the nations-standard and captor-deliverance panel. Its question and answer must remain together; atomizing verses 24-26 would produce a query without its rebuttal and detach the recognition statement from the rescue.

primary_reviews.support: The messenger formula and hand-signal imagery restart the speech, while the captive question is answered through the all-flesh conclusion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verses 22-23 also complete the child-return imagery begun in Zion's preceding complaint.

primary_reviews.support: Nations procession, royal fosterage, captive disputation, and recognition form a compact answer panel with its own internal resolution.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Because the first image answers 49:14-21, the sibling relation must remain visible even with a separate chunk.

primary_reviews.support: The retrieval premortem sees unresolved continuity from Zion's complaint through the legal questions of 50:1-3.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Formula and question-answer evidence support the local unit, but only under compulsory 49:14-50:3 context.

challenge.claim: The children-and-captors panel may be misleading without the larger Zion-to-legal sequence.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Keep 49:22-26 searchable only with mandatory hydration through 49:14-50:3.

repairs.defensible_basis: The divine legal questions about a divorce document and creditors begin at 50:1, shift to the absence of an answer, and culminate in sea-drying and heavenly-darkness claims. Verse 4 then changes to a first-person taught-tongue testimony with a different form.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 50:1-3 as a legal disputation ending in a creation-power answer. Family imagery links backward to Zion, but imagery alone cannot erase the chapter-opening questions or merge them into the disciple's first-person speech.

primary_reviews.support: Interrogatives about bill, creditor, calling, and shortened hand govern verses 1-2; first-person power claims in verses 2-3 answer them.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The abrupt transition at verse 4 is clear, while the backward addressee relation to Zion is less explicit.

primary_reviews.support: A legal accusation is followed by rhetorical proof of redeeming power, producing a complete question-and-answer disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit is very short and therefore depends on the 49:14-50:3 parent for its family-personification context.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical and retrieval review emphasizes the uninterrupted Zion-family problem across the chapter seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The new legal form remains defensible as a child if its upstream complaint and restoration answer travel with it.

challenge.claim: Separating 50:1-3 may conceal that the mother and children imagery continues from chapter 49.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Never surface 50:1-3 without the 49:14-50:3 operational parent.

repairs.defensible_basis: The taught-tongue testimony begins at verse 4 and proceeds through opened ear, suffering, help, and courtroom confidence; verses 10-11 then address two audiences as the testimony's practical alternatives. The self-lit-fire warning closes the governed speech.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 50:4-11 as one disciple-servant testimony with its audience exhortations. The verse-10 vocative is a strong internal seam, but cutting there would detach the two responses from the witness that defines whom they are asked to trust.

primary_reviews.support: The mi-bakhem question at 50:10 changes from first-person testimony to direct audience address, providing credible child-boundary evidence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The warning at verse 11 still depends on the preceding servant voice and shares the unit's final evaluative function.

challenge.claim: Verses 10-11 may form a distinct audience-exhortation child.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Test 50:4-9 and 50:10-11 as children, but require the complete 50:4-11 parent and avoid speaker identification.

primary_reviews.support: The primary distinguishes testimony in 4-9 from audience alternatives in 10-11 because person, addressee, and function change.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A whole-unit presentation better protects the exhortations from becoming detached moral sayings.

challenge.claim: The direct question in 50:10 opens a new rhetorical form.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Permit two hydrated children if downstream retrieval can always supply both siblings.

primary_reviews.support: Later reuse of suffering and trust language cannot decide the testimony-exhortation seam or the speaker's identity.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-reference pressure makes form-based hydration more important, not less.

repairs.defensible_basis: Three coordinated listening summonses address pursuers of righteousness, the people who know righteousness, and those fearing reproach; creation, instruction, and enduring salvation bind them. Verse 8 closes with moth-and-worm contrast before an awake appeal changes the voice.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 51:1-8 as a three-summons comfort sequence. Atomizing each command would lose the cumulative movement from ancestral consolation through cosmic reversal to durable salvation, while verse 9 begins an unmistakable apostrophe to the divine arm.

primary_reviews.support: Repeated shim'u and haqshivu imperatives structure three linked panels, ending with the enduring-righteousness declaration in verse 8.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Different addressees and imperatives could justify internal indexing, but they remain coordinated within one reassurance sequence.

primary_reviews.support: The calls develop one argument: look to origins, attend coming instruction, and resist human reproach because salvation endures.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The sequence's internal triad should remain visible as stanza metadata rather than be erased by a single generic label.

primary_reviews.support: Abraham, creation, and salvation relations enrich the summonses without fixing separate retrieval units.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Familiar canonical themes could encourage extraction of one panel apart from its cumulative comfort logic.

repairs.defensible_basis: The doubled 'awake' addresses the arm of YHWH, recalls sea-monster and exodus imagery, and resolves in the returning-ransomed refrain. Verse 12 answers with an emphatic divine 'I, I,' making the voice change an actual seam rather than a chapter convenience.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 51:9-11 as an apostrophe and return refrain. Merging it unmarked with 51:12-16 would confuse appeal with answer; splitting the exodus images from the return line would leave the petition without its envisioned result.

primary_reviews.support: Uri-uri is a direct feminine imperative to the arm, whereas anokhi anokhi at 51:12 begins a first-person comfort response.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The return refrain also appears elsewhere in Isaiah and could be mistaken for a detachable liturgical fragment.

primary_reviews.support: A plea to awaken, remembered victory, and a confident return stanza form one short call whose answering voice follows immediately.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its dependence on 51:12-16 requires sibling hydration even though the boundary between voices is clear.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem specifically favored distinguishing the arm appeal from the divine answer while retaining their relation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Exodus and later reuse remain contextual parallels, not permission to isolate Rahab or the ransomed refrain.

repairs.defensible_basis: The emphatic 'I, I am your comforter' answers the preceding appeal, challenges fear of mortals, recalls the maker, and ends by placing words in the addressee's mouth with 'you are my people.' The cup summons at verse 17 addresses Jerusalem anew.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 51:12-16 as the divine comfort answer. Its speaker formula and people declaration enclose the response; joining it to 51:9 would erase appeal-and-answer form, while extending to 51:17 would cross a fresh city vocative.

primary_reviews.support: Anokhi anokhi marks an emphatic answer, and the covenantal speech reaches a syntactic close in the words-in-mouth and people declaration.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Pronoun and addressee interpretation within verse 16 remains difficult even though the outer boundary is strong.

primary_reviews.support: The response moves from comfort through fear correction and creator memory to a renewed relation, answering rather than continuing the apostrophe.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its rhetoric depends on the preceding plea, so independent retrieval must include the awake-arm sibling.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical-premortem review endorsed the 51:9-11 appeal and 51:12-16 answer distinction under a shared parent.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-references to creation or covenant cannot settle the difficult internal pronouns.

repairs.defensible_basis: The second awake command now addresses Jerusalem, develops the cup-of-wrath image through desolation and helpless sons, and reverses the cup onto tormentors. That transfer completes the city oracle before Zion receives a new awake command in 52:1.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 51:17-23 as Jerusalem's cup-reversal speech. The repeated image binds accusation and rescue across all seven verses; extending across the chapter would combine two different awake addresses, while splitting at the rescue would sever reversal from crisis.

primary_reviews.support: Hit'oreri and qumi address Jerusalem directly, and the cup vocabulary continues until it is transferred in verse 23.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The following uri-uri to Zion repeats awakening language and creates a close sibling rather than unrelated material.

primary_reviews.support: City summons, devastation report, double calamity, announced advocacy, and cup transfer form a complete reversal oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit should retain its 51:17-52:6 paired-city parent because the next speech carries restoration forward.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem rejected the old 51:9-52:12 superchunk and recognized this cup-reversal movement separately.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical cup imagery supplies comparison only and must not determine the seam.

repairs.defensible_basis: A second doubled awake summons now names Zion and Jerusalem, commands release from dust and bonds, and explains the people's sale, oppression, and coming recognition of the divine name. Verse 7's herald scene replaces direct city address with an arriving messenger.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 52:1-6 as an awake-Zion redemption oracle. The name-recognition promise is its explanatory close; merging it into the herald poem would blur a direct imperative to the city with the narrator's celebration of good news on the mountains.

primary_reviews.support: Uri-uri followed by Zion and Jerusalem vocatives opens the speech, while 'my people shall know my name' finishes the divine explanation in verse 6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The repeated awakening vocabulary deliberately relates this unit to 51:17-23 and should not be treated as a wholly new macro-cycle.

primary_reviews.support: Enthronement clothing, release commands, historical explanation, and promised name recognition produce a complete redemption address.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The prose-like explanation in verses 3-6 shifts texture but remains governed by the city's awakening summons.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem identified 52:1-6 between Jerusalem's cup reversal and the herald proclamation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later Zion and redemption parallels cannot replace the local vocatives as seam evidence.

repairs.defensible_basis: The exclamation over beautiful feet introduces a mountain herald, watchmen answering together, Zion's comfort, and YHWH baring an arm before all nations. Universal sight in verse 10 finishes the proclamation; the doubled departure imperative at verse 11 starts a different action.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 52:7-10 as a herald-and-enthronement poem. Its watchmen and universal audience belong together, whereas separating famous herald language through later citation would fracture the movement before the bared-arm conclusion.

primary_reviews.support: Mah-na'wu begins the herald exclamation, and the chain from good news to watchmen to revealed arm closes with all ends seeing in verse 10.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The departure imperatives at 52:11 remain tightly related as the response expected from the announced reign.

primary_reviews.support: The literary primary groups herald, enthronement, and departure as 52:7-12 because proclamation and response form one exodus movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The new imperative sequence at verse 11 is sufficiently distinct to justify children if both remain hydrated.

challenge.claim: Verses 7-12 may be one proclamation-and-departure unit.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Preserve 52:7-12 as an operational parent over 52:7-10 and 52:11-12.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieval review favored separating herald proclamation from the guarded departure summons while keeping them adjacent.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical quotation of the herald must not narrow the unit to a single verse.

repairs.defensible_basis: The repeated 'depart' commands initiate a compact exodus summons: leave, touch no unclean thing, purify yourselves, and go without panic because YHWH leads and guards. Both verses are necessary; neither has a self-contained function when retrieved alone.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 52:11-12 as a departure coda under compulsory 51:1-52:12 hydration. The doubled imperative opens a new response to the herald, and the front-and-rear-guard statement closes it; a one-verse extraction would split command from assurance.

primary_reviews.support: Suru suru and tse'u are plural imperatives at 52:11, answered by front-guard and rear-guard participial claims in verse 12.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its brevity makes paragraph evidence insufficient for naked retrieval; parent and herald sibling are mandatory.

primary_reviews.support: The literary proposal retains 52:7-12 so the announcement and commanded departure remain one movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A discrete imperative form exists at verse 11, but it should not be presented without the herald.

challenge.claim: The two-verse summons may be an internal coda rather than an independent child.
challenge.proposed_remedy: If surfaced, always hydrate 52:11-12 with 52:7-10 and the 51:1-52:12 parent.

primary_reviews.support: The review recognized the departure summons as a distinct response but rejected naked verse retrieval.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Exodus parallels clarify function without granting either verse autonomous status.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'Behold, my servant shall act wisely' opens a presentation that passes through astonished nations, communal report, suffering, death, outcome, and a concluding divine allotment. The English chapter break interrupts no voice or form, and the final bearing-of-sin statement supplies the poem's close.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 52:13-53:12 as one servant poem at high boundary confidence while preserving textual uncertainty inside it. Chapter division and later quotation are both rejected as seam authorities; dividing the report from the concluding speech would dismantle the poem's answer structure.

primary_reviews.support: Hen yaskil 'avdi begins the presentation, first-person plural report dominates 53:1-6, and the final first-person allotment in 53:11-12 closes the frame.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC share a Leningrad-family base; they cannot independently resolve 52:15, 53:8, 53:10, or the WEB footnote about 'light' in 53:11.

primary_reviews.support: Presentation, audience reaction, communal confession, narrated suffering and burial, then evaluative conclusion constitute an indivisible poetic sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Many famous lines have independent reception histories, creating exceptional extraction pressure despite the coherent form.

primary_reviews.support: Extensive canonical reuse confirms dense relations but cannot create seams or decide the servant's identity.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A later quotation may begin or end midmovement, so its bounds must not be projected onto Isaiah.

repairs.defensible_basis: The barren woman's song-command opens a city restoration movement through enlarged tents, reversal of shame, renewed marriage imagery, flood comparison, and the covenant of peace. Verse 11 changes the addressee to an afflicted, storm-tossed city and begins the jeweled rebuilding panel.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 54:1-10 as the barren-Zion restoration and covenant reassurance. Ending with the unshaken peace covenant respects the completed marriage-and-mercy argument; whole-chapter retrieval alone would hide the new visual and architectural form at verse 11.

primary_reviews.support: Ranni 'aqarah is a feminine singular command, and the mercy-oath sequence reaches a covenantal close at 54:10.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: City and woman metaphors continue into verse 11, so the division reflects form change rather than a new referent ruling.

primary_reviews.support: Song, expansion, shame reversal, spouse reassurance, flood analogy, and peace covenant form a sustained restoration address.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A whole-chapter parent remains useful because both children portray the same afflicted-restored city.

primary_reviews.support: Covenant and flood relations illuminate the reassurance but do not determine the verse-10 endpoint.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later use of the barren-woman language could encourage extracting verse 1 from its complete restoration movement.

repairs.defensible_basis: The vocative 'afflicted, storm-tossed, and not comforted' resets the imagery to jeweled foundations, taught children, established righteousness, failed attackers, and the heritage of YHWH's servants. The final heritage declaration in verse 17 closes this city-protection oracle.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 54:11-17 as the jeweled-city and protected-servants panel. It has an independent address and concluding ownership formula; merging all chapter 54 would flatten the change from marital covenant reassurance to architecture, security, and communal heritage.

primary_reviews.support: The feminine vocative at 54:11 starts a new description, and the concluding zot nachalat 'avde YHWH formula marks ownership and closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The same city addressee continues from 54:1-10, limiting how independently this child should be presented.

primary_reviews.support: Jeweled construction, taught descendants, righteousness, failed weapons, and servant heritage comprise a complete protected-city oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later interpretations of the stones or servants cannot decide the city's identity or subdivide the list.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical city and foundation imagery is relation evidence only; it neither names the community nor sets an internal seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The protected-servants close may be quoted separately, so hydration with the afflicted-city opening is important.

repairs.defensible_basis: The cry to everyone who thirsts initiates an invitation to water, food, attentive hearing, life, covenant, and nations; the unknown nation's running response completes the appeal in verse 5. The seek command in verse 6 changes from invitation and covenant offer to urgent return.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 55:1-5 as the water-food invitation and covenant appeal. The nations-running conclusion belongs with the David covenant statement it develops, while retaining all chapter 55 would conceal the new imperative, wicked-person address, and creation procession that follow.

primary_reviews.support: Hoy kol-tsame begins a public invitation, and the covenant-witness-nations syntax reaches its result in the running nation of verse 5.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The imperative series continues at verse 6, so the two halves remain closely coordinated within chapter 55.

primary_reviews.support: Invitation, rhetorical challenge, listening, covenant assurance, witness language, and international response form one offer sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Food and water images tempt devotional extraction, but their literary function depends on hearing and covenant.

primary_reviews.support: Davidic and nations relations are context for the invitation; they do not establish where the next exhortation begins.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later citation of the thirst invitation cannot reduce the unit to its opening verse.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'Seek YHWH while he may be found' begins an exhortation to return, explains divine compassion and the distance between thoughts, compares the effective word to rain, and ends with joyful departure and an everlasting sign. The sequence proceeds from human response to divine efficacy and creation's answer.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 55:6-13 as a seek-return and effective-word procession. Isolating the thoughts or word sayings would break their argumentative placement between repentance and transformed creation; verse 13's sign statement supplies the actual terminus.

primary_reviews.support: Dirshu and the return imperatives open the section, while the ki-asher comparison develops through word accomplishment to the everlasting-sign close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Several proverb-like lines can appear self-contained in translation, but their Hebrew connectors maintain the argument.

primary_reviews.support: Exhortation, mercy rationale, thought comparison, rain-word analogy, and celebratory exodus make a carefully linked movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift from direct address to extended simile is internal development, not evidence for famous-saying chunks.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical uses of divine word or exodus imagery cannot select an internal boundary in this argument.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retrieval must keep the effective-word analogy attached to both return and its creation-level outcome.

repairs.defensible_basis: A messenger formula introduces commands to keep justice and righteousness, a Sabbath beatitude, speeches to foreigner and eunuch, a promised memorial, and an ingathering declaration. 'I will gather others to him' in verse 8 completes the widening movement before beasts are summoned against failed watchmen.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 56:1-8 as a justice-Sabbath and outsider-gathering oracle. The unit's boundary follows addressee and form, not a policy conclusion; extending into verse 9 would cross from promised inclusion to animal summons and leadership satire.

primary_reviews.support: Koh amar YHWH begins the exhortation, and the participial gatherer formula in verse 8 closes the foreigner-eunuch-gathering sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Terms for Sabbath, foreigner, eunuch, and memorial carry translation and social-context questions that do not invalidate the outer seam.

primary_reviews.support: Justice command, blessing, two anticipated objections, direct reassurance, house-of-prayer promise, and final gathering claim form a complete inclusion oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The list could be overatomized by addressee; the repeated gathering purpose keeps it whole.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical and policy questions lie outside the chunking authority and cannot determine this boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The retrieval rationale must avoid turning the selected unit into a normative ruling about later communities.

repairs.defensible_basis: The beast summons at 56:9 opens a satire on blind watchmen, mute dogs, greedy shepherds, and their drinking boast; 57:1-2 then notices the righteous person's death and rest. Because that notice can either condemn public indifference or begin a new contrast, the cross-chapter parent remains held.
repairs.boss_rationale: Hold 56:9-57:2 as the surfaced unit rather than force a verse-boundary answer. Splitting at the chapter would separate the righteous-death notice from the failed-leader context it may close, yet folding it permanently backward would conceal a plausible transition toward 57:3.

primary_reviews.support: The beast vocative and participial watchmen satire are clear, but ha-tsaddiq 'avad at 57:1 changes subject abruptly and can initiate a new observation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Correlated OSHB and UXLC views cannot provide independent witness convergence for the discourse attachment.

challenge.claim: The function of 57:1-2 relative to the watchmen satire remains unsettled.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Compare 56:9-12 plus 57:1-2 children against the held parent using independent Hebrew discourse evidence.

primary_reviews.support: Leadership satire followed by ignored righteous death makes a coherent indictment-and-consequence reading at the larger level.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A separately retrievable death-and-rest notice is also a defensible form if the failed-watchmen parent always accompanies it.

primary_reviews.support: Premortem review identified this exact cross-chapter attachment as a hot zone and rejected silent chapter fallback.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Relations to other shepherd or righteous-death passages cannot decide whether the notice closes or opens.

repairs.defensible_basis: The command 'draw near here' addresses a new accusatory audience and develops mockery, cultic sites, bed imagery, diplomatic journeys, exposure, and a final contrast between wind-carried works and refuge. The refuge-inheritance sentence at verse 13 closes the prosecution.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 57:3-13 as an idolatrous-offspring accusation. Its direct vocative distinguishes it from the death notice, and the wind-versus-refuge verdict finishes the case; keeping only a 56:9-57:13 superchunk would bury this sharp addressee reset.

primary_reviews.support: We'atem qirvu-hennah opens a direct plural accusation, and the wind/refuge antithesis completes it in 57:13.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Rare cultic and sexual euphemisms introduce translation uncertainty inside the speech without weakening its outer address.

primary_reviews.support: Vocative, taunting questions, location catalogue, political-cultic exposure, and refuge contrast constitute a full accusation oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Individual images must not become tiny chunks because their force accumulates toward the closing verdict.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem required separation from 56:9-57:2 while preserving the 56:9-57:13 context relation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Other idolatry passages may clarify imagery but cannot set this seam or identify historical groups.

repairs.defensible_basis: The road-building imperative initiates a proclamation about the high and holy one dwelling with the contrite, limits divine contention, recounts wrath and healing, and contrasts peace with the tossing wicked sea. The no-peace statement at verse 21 provides a deliberate refrain-like close.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 57:14-21 as a road-building and contrite-healing oracle ending in contrast. Dividing healing from the wicked-sea conclusion would remove the negative foil that completes the promise; extending backward would cross the refuge verdict and a new proclamation form.

primary_reviews.support: Solu solu and pannu-derekh open with plural imperatives, while 'no peace' seals the righteous/wicked contrast in verse 21.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: First-person shifts between wrath, hiding, seeing, and healing make internal movements but not separate speeches.

primary_reviews.support: Preparation command, transcendence-and-contrition claim, limited wrath, healing, created praise, and sea contrast form one balanced oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The positive healing panel could be excerpted, but the final contrast supplies its literary completion.

primary_reviews.support: Peace and contrition relations do not establish an internal boundary or decide the subjects addressed.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The no-peace refrain also connects to 48:22, a relation that should not merge noncontiguous units.

repairs.defensible_basis: The cry-aloud commission opens a dispute over apparent devotion and fasting, contrasts exploitation with release and care, then develops conditional light, guidance, rebuilding, and restored-path names. Verse 12 completes the justice-to-restoration argument before a new Sabbath condition begins.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 58:1-12 as the false-fast and justice disputation with its promised outcomes. Ending before verse 13 preserves the difference between the communal fast critique and the separate foot-and-Sabbath condition; whole-chapter retrieval would hide that functional reset.

primary_reviews.support: Qera be-garon begins the prophetic commission, repeated interrogatives structure the fast dispute, and rebuilding titles finish the conditional result in verse 12.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The if-then syntax continues in 58:13, so the chapter remains a strong operational parent.

primary_reviews.support: Complaint, counter-question, social indictment, chosen-fast definition, and restoration consequences form a complete disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The long result catalogue could be mistaken for several oracles, but it remains dependent on the preceding conditions.

primary_reviews.support: Review explicitly favored 58:1-12 and a separate Sabbath coda rather than one chapter fallback.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ethical parallels elsewhere cannot authorize the seam or turn chunking into a policy judgment.

repairs.defensible_basis: The conditional 'if you turn your foot from the Sabbath' introduces a compact coda about speech, delight, riding high, and feeding on Jacob's heritage. The mouth-of-YHWH formula closes it, but the two verses require chapter-parent hydration and should never appear as a naked saying.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 58:13-14 as a Sabbath conditional coda with mandatory 58:1-14 context. Its new condition and formal divine close justify retrieval, while isolation would detach the promise from the chapter's preceding critique of performative devotion.

primary_reviews.support: Im-tashiv introduces a new conditional protasis, and ki pi YHWH dibber supplies an explicit speech close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Two-verse brevity and shared conditional rhetoric with verses 1-12 argue against unhydrated presentation.

primary_reviews.support: Foot, speech, delight, elevation, and inheritance constitute a concise conditional coda distinct from the fast disputation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its independence is functional rather than thematic; without the chapter parent it can be misconstrued as an isolated rule.

primary_reviews.support: Premortem review accepted the seam but questioned whether the coda should ever surface independently.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The explicit closing formula supports a child, provided retrieval always includes the fast-and-justice sibling.

challenge.claim: The Sabbath coda may be internal-only despite its formal closure.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Enforce 58:1-14 hydration and prohibit naked 58:13-14 retrieval.

repairs.defensible_basis: The declaration that YHWH's hand is not shortened answers an implied objection, then attributes separation to wrongdoing and expands into hands, lips, courts, eggs, webs, violent feet, and crooked paths. The no-peace conclusion at verse 8 ends the second-person indictment before 'therefore justice is far from us' changes to communal confession.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 59:1-8 as ability defense and wrongdoing indictment. The person shift at verse 9 is a genuine seam; merging the confession would collapse accusation and self-inclusion, while stopping earlier would fragment a single governed catalogue.

primary_reviews.support: Hen lo-qatsrah opens the ability defense, second- and third-person accusations dominate, and the crooked-path/no-peace close precedes a first-person plural turn.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Catalogue density produces many internal poetic lines, but none resets the governing indictment.

primary_reviews.support: Objection, causal answer, body-part catalogue, failed justice, hatching-weaving images, and violent path conclusion form one accusation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The vivid metaphors should remain internal features rather than become individually retrievable sayings.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical sin and path parallels do not decide where accusation becomes confession in Isaiah 59.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The first-person plural shift is stronger local evidence than any later quotation.

repairs.defensible_basis: The communal 'therefore justice is far from us' begins confession and lament, but verse 15 turns inside the verse from missing truth to YHWH seeing and being displeased; intervention, armor, repayment, a redeemer, and covenant then follow. Verse granularity cannot represent the 15a/15b pivot honestly.
repairs.boss_rationale: Hold 59:9-21 as the active confession-to-intervention parent. A 9-15 and 16-21 split would assign the latter half of verse 15 to the wrong movement, yet ignoring the turn would erase two real forms; independent clause-sensitive review must choose the presentation.

primary_reviews.support: At 59:15 the waw clause 'YHWH saw' begins divine observation after the communal account of absent truth; the pivot is intra-verse.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC expose the same Leningrad-family wording, so they do not constitute independent textual confirmation.

challenge.claim: A verse-only route cannot place the confession/intervention seam exactly.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Compare whole 59:9-21 against disclosed approximate children 59:9-15 and 59:16-21 with external Hebrew review.

primary_reviews.support: Confession and divine-warrior intervention are distinct literary movements, and the latter begins before verse 16.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Keeping the larger unit avoids a false exact seam but reduces direct retrieval of the two forms.

challenge.claim: The active parent suppresses a genuine midverse form change.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Retain the hold until clause-level boundaries or an explicit approximation policy is authorized.

primary_reviews.support: The premortem preferred whole 59:1-21 at verse granularity or a disclosed hold rather than a confident split.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Redeemer and covenant relations later in canon cannot repair the local midverse problem.

challenge.claim: Canonical reuse may bias reviewers toward starting the intervention too late.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Adjudicate only from Isaiah's discourse and direct textual evidence, with 59:15b named explicitly.

repairs.defensible_basis: The arise-and-shine command opens Zion's illumination, nations and kings approaching, children returning, abundance arriving, and ships bringing sons from afar. Verse 9 completes the first maritime procession; foreign builders and open gates begin a new city-administration panel at verse 10.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 60:1-9 as the illumination and gathering procession. A whole-chapter chunk would hide the transition from arriving peoples and ships to reconstruction, gate policy, and renamed civic space, while extracting light verses would sever them from the returning children.

primary_reviews.support: Qumi ori is a feminine city summons; deictic gathering and sea-wealth language proceed through the ships and sons in verse 9.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 10 continues nations-and-kings material, so the seam depends on movement and function rather than a wholly new addressee.

primary_reviews.support: Light, nations, children, abundance, animal procession, and ships form an arrival sequence that reaches a visible pause.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The catalogue can feel expansive enough to absorb the chapter, but later verses shift from procession to rebuilt city order.

primary_reviews.support: Later light and nations imagery supplies relations but no independent verse-9 boundary.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Famous arise-shine retrieval is a major premortem risk unless the gathering procession travels with it.

repairs.defensible_basis: Foreigners building walls and kings serving the city open a new administrative panel: gates remain open, hostile nations face judgment, wealth enters, former oppressors bow, and violence gives way to renamed walls and gates. The paired names Salvation and Praise finish the transformation at verse 18.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 60:10-18 as the rebuilding-and-transformed-city movement. Verse 19 starts a different everlasting-light coda with the sun and moon; merging it here would blur civic reconstruction and renaming with a new cosmic illumination claim.

primary_reviews.support: The subject shift to foreign builders at 60:10 begins the panel, and the naming clause for walls and gates gives verse 18 a formal civic close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Nations and kings continue from verses 1-9, so the unit remains a functional child of the full Zion procession.

primary_reviews.support: Construction, open gates, tribute, reversed domination, material transformation, and renamed defenses form a complete city-order sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The many catalogue items should not be separated merely because each has vivid imagery.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical city and gate parallels offer hydration but cannot establish the verse-18 ending.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later ideal-city imagery could cause thematic mega-clustering across the clear light reset at verse 19.

repairs.defensible_basis: The declaration that sun and moon will no longer provide the city's light begins a compact finale about everlasting illumination, ended mourning, universal righteousness, enduring possession, and accelerated growth. 'I, YHWH, will hasten it' closes the chapter and the panel.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 60:19-22 as the everlasting-light coda. Its cosmic-light opening is not another item in the building catalogue, and extracting only verse 19 would lose the mourning, people, land, and divine-timing conclusions that complete the stanza.

primary_reviews.support: Lo-yihyeh-lakh 'od begins a negative future contrast with prior city conditions, and the first-person hastening statement closes verse 22.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Light imagery links backward to 60:1, making the whole chapter a strong ring-shaped parent.

primary_reviews.support: Cosmic illumination, transformed mourning, righteous inhabitants, planted possession, and accelerated population create a short chapter finale.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Because every line is memorable, the risk is verse-level extraction rather than undersegmentation.

primary_reviews.support: Later canonical light imagery cannot decide whether Isaiah's coda starts at verse 19 or identify its subjects.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The local no-longer contrast and chapter-closing divine signature remain the proper evidence.

repairs.defensible_basis: The first-person report 'the Spirit of the Lord YHWH is on me' introduces an anointing and a chain of proclamation assignments to the poor, brokenhearted, captives, mourners, and Zion. The naming of oaks of righteousness and the purpose of divine glory complete the commission in verse 3.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 61:1-3 as a proclamation commission without identifying the speaker. Verse 4 changes from first-person task report to third-person rebuilding outcomes; later quotation may illuminate reception but cannot shorten or redefine Isaiah's complete commission.

primary_reviews.support: Ruah Adonai YHWH 'alay opens the self-report, and the infinitive chain ends in naming and planting purpose at 61:3.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: WEB notes an addition associated with LXX and DSS, but no pinned local primary LXX or DSS text is available to adjudicate wording.

primary_reviews.support: Anointing, commissioned announcements, reversals for mourners, new names, and a final glory purpose form one recognizable vocation speech.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The identity of the first-person voice is disputed and must remain separate from the form decision.

primary_reviews.support: Later citation of part of the commission neither supplies a local Isaiah seam nor settles the speaker.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Quotation bounds create a strong premortem hazard if projected backward onto verses 1-3.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'They shall rebuild the old ruins' changes from commission to communal outcomes: reconstruction, changed labor relations, priestly naming, double inheritance, justice, covenant, and recognized offspring. The public recognition statement in verse 9 closes that promise sequence.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 61:4-9 as a rebuilding, reversal, and covenant panel. Whole-chapter treatment would hide the shift to first-person rejoicing at verse 10, while splitting the social catalogue would detach its items from the covenant and recognized-seed resolution.

primary_reviews.support: The third-person we-banu opening begins new activity, and the recognized-offspring clause in verse 9 completes the public-outcome panel.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Speaker and pronoun changes inside verses 7-8 are difficult but do not displace the outer shift at verses 4 and 10.

primary_reviews.support: Ruins, labor, role reversal, inheritance, justice, covenant, and offspring recognition form one restoration-result sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Individual social reversals may receive separate canonical attention, yet their function here is cumulative.

primary_reviews.support: Priestly, covenantal, and inheritance parallels cannot assign a boundary or identify a later community.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retrieval should preserve the entire reversal catalogue rather than select one institutionally charged line.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'I will greatly rejoice in YHWH' introduces a new first-person praise, using garments, bridegroom, bride, earth, and garden to celebrate righteousness and praise springing before nations. The two-verse hymn is complete but requires chapter and sibling hydration because its speaker is not identified.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 61:10-11 as a garment-and-garden praise coda. The emphatic rejoicing voice distinguishes it from the preceding plural promises; merging all chapter 61 would conceal that lyrical response, while naked retrieval would invite an unwarranted speaker ruling.

primary_reviews.support: Sos asis begins emphatic first-person rejoicing, and the earth-garden comparison carries the praise to the chapter close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The shift does not identify whether the voice is individual, Zion, or communal; form alone cannot answer that question.

primary_reviews.support: Clothing and wedding similes lead into a germination image, creating a concise responsive hymn after the restoration promises.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Two-verse scale makes compulsory connection to 61:1-9 essential for responsible retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical garment, bride, and garden relations do not name the speaker or create smaller seams.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The coda's independence is literary, not permission to isolate an identity claim.

repairs.defensible_basis: The vow not to be silent for Zion opens a movement toward visible righteousness, royal recognition, a new name, a crown, reversal of abandonment names, and marriage rejoicing. The bridegroom simile at verse 5 completes the renaming-and-delight argument before watchmen are introduced.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 62:1-5 as Zion vindication, renaming, and marriage oracle. Verse 6 replaces the vow with installed watchmen and their charge; retaining the full chapter as one unit would hide this functional handoff.

primary_reviews.support: Lema'an Tsiyyon lo eheseh initiates the vow, and the final bridegroom comparison resolves the Hephzibah-Beulah renaming in verse 5.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Zion remains the common subject through chapter 62, so the seam distinguishes rhetorical tasks rather than topics.

primary_reviews.support: Prophetic resolve, dawning vindication, public naming, crown imagery, reversed epithets, and marriage joy make a complete city oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The new-name sequence must stay together; atomizing individual names would destroy its reversal logic.

primary_reviews.support: Marriage and city-name relations elsewhere cannot decide Isaiah's internal unit or the vow's speaker.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later reception should not turn the boundary into an identification of Zion or the rejoicing figure.

repairs.defensible_basis: The declaration that watchmen have been set on Jerusalem's walls begins a charge to constant remembrance and prayer, followed by YHWH's oath that grain and wine will no longer feed enemies. Eating and drinking in the sacred courts complete the watchmen-and-harvest assurance.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 62:6-9 as a watchmen charge joined to its sworn food-security answer. Verse 10 turns to gate-passing and highway commands; merging that procession would obscure the distinction between intercessory vigilance and public preparation.

primary_reviews.support: The wall-watchmen clause introduces new agents, and the oath formula governs grain and wine until the court-consumption close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Watchmen and oath panels could be indexed internally, but the promise is the answer to their unceasing charge.

primary_reviews.support: Appointment, no-silence command, pressure for Jerusalem's establishment, divine oath, and secured harvest form a compact assurance movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The repeated imperatives at verse 10 constitute a stronger new action than any internal division here.

primary_reviews.support: Watchman and oath parallels supply context but do not determine separate chunks in 62:6-9.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Retrieval must avoid treating the oath as an independent promise detached from the charged watchers.

repairs.defensible_basis: The repeated commands to pass through gates, prepare a people's way, build a highway, remove stones, raise a banner, and proclaim to the earth launch the final procession panel. The four closing city-and-people names finish both the command and chapter.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 62:10-12 as a highway-herald and naming finale. Its imperative barrage clearly begins after the harvest oath; splitting each name or proclamation would dismantle a single preparation-and-arrival sequence.

primary_reviews.support: Ivru ivru and sollu sollu create a new plural command cluster, while the final naming predicates provide closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Short commands and titles are internally segmented but function together as one procession preparation.

primary_reviews.support: Gate passage, road work, banner, global announcement, arriving reward, and new designations complete the chapter's public movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The names have lexical interest but no independent scene, speaker, or action warranting separate retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Highway and herald relations elsewhere do not decide this local span or authorize name-by-name extraction.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The chapter's three children need a common 62:1-12 parent to preserve their progression.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'Who is this coming from Edom?' creates a question-and-answer scene about location, garments, strength, winepress, solitude, anger, and recompense. The warrior's final statement about pouring lifeblood on the earth ends the dialogue before a new communal remembrance begins at verse 7.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 63:1-6 as the Edom-warrior dialogue without deciding the figure's identity or endorsing an ethical judgment. The Q-and-A frame and winepress monologue are inseparable; extending into verse 7 would cross from violent self-report to remembered mercies.

primary_reviews.support: Mi-zeh opens an interrogative encounter, alternating questions and first-person answers until the completed recompense account in verse 6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Rare color, blood, and winepress vocabulary creates translation pressure but no stronger internal seam.

primary_reviews.support: Arrival question, clothing question, solitary winepress explanation, appointed time, absent helper, and result constitute one dramatic dialogue.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The violence imagery must not be used to identify the speaker or convert the boundary into moral adjudication.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical warrior and winepress relations cannot identify this figure or alter Isaiah's dialogue frame.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later imagery may intensify extraction pressure around individual lines, so the complete exchange must remain intact.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'I will mention the loving kindnesses of YHWH' changes voice and purpose from the warrior scene to remembered mercy, peoplehood, affliction, rebellion, remembered exodus, guidance, rest, and a glorious name. Verse 14 completes the historical praise before direct petition begins.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 63:7-14 as remembered-mercies and exodus praise. The 'look down from heaven' appeal at verse 15 creates the next mode; merging it backward would confuse narrated memory with present prayer, while ending early would truncate the guided-rest conclusion.

primary_reviews.support: Hasde YHWH azkirah starts first-person praise, and the historical we/they sequence reaches the glorious-name purpose in verse 14.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Isaiah 63:9 contains textual and translation pressure that correlated local Hebrew views cannot independently settle.

primary_reviews.support: Mercy recital, filial expectation, affliction, rebellion, remembered deliverance, guided descent, and rest make a compact historical hymn.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The exodus recollection supplies the basis for the following plea, requiring a strong sibling relation.

primary_reviews.support: Exodus and wilderness parallels illuminate the recital but do not set a seam or harmonize wording.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The remembered history should not be divided according to later quotations of its components.

repairs.defensible_basis: The imperative to look down from heaven begins a communal lament that appeals to divine kinship, asks why wandering persists, pleads for a torn-heavens descent, confesses sin, invokes potter and people imagery, surveys ruined cities, and ends with unanswered questions. The prayer crosses the English chapter seam without changing voice.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 63:15-64:12 as one communal lament-prayer at high unit confidence, while lowering textual certainty inside it. A chapter split would sever the theophany plea from its kinship appeal; smaller famous-line units would fragment confession and the final appeal for response.

primary_reviews.support: Habbet mi-shamayim establishes the petition, and first-person plural address persists to the closing questions; however 63:19-64:1 versification and 63:9 textual pressure limit finer adjudication.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC are correlated Leningrad-family representations, not independent witnesses for disputed wording or clause attachment.

primary_reviews.support: Heavenward appeal, father claim, wandering question, theophany request, remembered acts, confession, potter metaphor, devastation, and final interrogation form one prayer.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal turns are substantial, but none changes the praying community or resolves before the last question.

primary_reviews.support: Later use of the theophany and waiting language cannot dictate a chapter seam or a preferred textual reading.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit should expose its WEB-MT versification caution whenever retrieved.

repairs.defensible_basis: The divine answer opens with being sought and found by those not calling, then catalogs a continually provoking people through gardens, tombs, prohibited foods, separation claims, smoke imagery, and a measured promise to repay ancestral and present acts. Verse 8 starts a preservation analogy rather than continuing the indictment list.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 65:1-7 as the answer-and-provocation catalogue. The measured-recompense sentence finishes the accusation; retaining 65:1-16 would hide the new-wine analogy and servants-versus-you structure that deliberately qualifies judgment.

primary_reviews.support: Nidrashti and nimtseti begin first-person response, and the measurement/recompense syntax closes the catalogue in verse 7.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The verbal voice and addressee of 65:1 are translation-sensitive, so the boundary cannot authorize an interpretation of who sought whom.

primary_reviews.support: Answer, outstretched-hands image, cultic-location catalogue, quoted separation, smoke, written record, and repayment form a complete indictment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 8's cluster image creates a conspicuous rhetorical reset toward preservation and contrast.

primary_reviews.support: Later citation of 65:1 bears on reception but cannot identify the audience or fix internal seams.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The provocative practices should remain a governed catalogue rather than separate issue-based chunks.

repairs.defensible_basis: The new-wine-in-a-cluster analogy begins a preservation movement, promises descendants and chosen possession, and contrasts servants with those who forsake YHWH through food, drink, joy, song, naming, and oath reversals. Forgotten former troubles close the contrast at verse 16.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 65:8-16 as the preserved-cluster and servants contrast. The analogy and repeated servant-versus-you pairs belong together; mapping those groups onto later communities would exceed chunking authority, and merging 1-16 would suppress the preservation reset.

primary_reviews.support: Ka'asher yimmatse ha-tirosh introduces the cluster analogy, while the oath and forgotten-troubles language completes the servant contrast.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Group labels and second-person references remain interpretation-sensitive even though the repeated syntax is clear.

primary_reviews.support: Preservation analogy, chosen inheritance, abandoned table, four paired reversals, new naming, and forgotten distress create a controlled antiphonal oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The servant contrasts invite atomization, but their rhetorical force depends on cumulative parallelism.

primary_reviews.support: Canonical servant or remnant relations cannot identify the groups or choose a doctrinal reading.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The active seam rests on the cluster reset and repeated contrast, not later community mapping.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth' launches a creation oracle about forgotten former things, Jerusalem's joy, transformed lifespan, secure labor, answered prayer, animal peace, and the holy-mountain close. The chapter's final clause completes the catalogue before a throne-temple disputation begins.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 65:17-25 as a new-creation and transformed-life oracle. Later apocalyptic reuse does not create a seam within Isaiah; separating lifespan, labor, prayer, or animal images would dismantle the single created-world vision.

primary_reviews.support: Hineni bore opens the creation declaration, and the lo-yare'u formula on the holy mountain closes verse 25.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Lifespan language in verse 20 and several verbal forms require translation caution without weakening the full oracle frame.

primary_reviews.support: New creation, city joy, reversed mortality, secure building and planting, answered call, and animal peace form one visionary catalogue.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Each image has substantial reception history, creating a predictable risk of theme-based microchunks.

primary_reviews.support: Later new-creation texts are relation evidence only and cannot dictate Isaiah's internal bounds.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The unit must remain non-authorizing about eschatological sequence or fulfillment.

repairs.defensible_basis: A throne-and-footstool declaration opens questions about building and rest, contrasts divine making with regard for the humble word-trembler, then reverses sacrificial acts and ends with chosen delusions because no one answered. Verse 5 addresses word-tremblers directly and begins another voice.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 66:1-4 as a throne-temple and worship disputation. The chosen-delusions verdict closes the call-and-response failure; extending to verse 6 would mix indirect contrast with a direct community address, while the boundary itself authorizes no anti-temple theology.

primary_reviews.support: Koh amar YHWH frames throne and house questions, and the ya'an clause explains the verdict through nonresponse at verse 4.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Sacrificial comparisons in verse 3 are syntactically dense and ethically charged, but they remain inside the disputation.

primary_reviews.support: Cosmic throne claim, house challenge, humble-person contrast, ritual reversals, and failed-call judgment make a complete argument.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The form must not be reduced to a topical temple passage or divided by each ritual example.

primary_reviews.support: Temple relations elsewhere cannot convert this chunk boundary into a judgment on worship or sacred space.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The direct word-trembler address at verse 5 is stronger seam evidence than broad temple themes.

repairs.defensible_basis: 'Hear the word of YHWH, you who tremble at his word' introduces a persecuted audience, quotes hostile brothers, promises their shame, and then locates a tumultuous recompense voice in city and temple. The two verses operate as an address-and-soundscape hinge before Zion's birth poem.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 66:5-6 as a word-tremblers and temple-recompense unit under final-cycle hydration. Merging through verse 16 would swallow the birth-and-comfort form; retrieving either verse alone would separate the audience promise from its audible outcome.

primary_reviews.support: Shim'u debar YHWH with an explicit word-trembler vocative opens verse 5, and the triple qol sequence resolves in recompense at verse 6.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The brief hinge shares temple vocabulary backward and enemy judgment forward, so parent context is indispensable.

primary_reviews.support: Audience address, quoted mockery, promised appearance, and escalating city-temple-divine voices constitute a compact transitional oracle.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its two-verse scale should not conceal the genuine speaker and scene reset before verse 7.

primary_reviews.support: Word-trembler and temple parallels do not establish an independent retrieval level for these verses.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Any surface must include siblings on both sides to avoid turning the hinge into a free-standing promise.

repairs.defensible_basis: The paradoxical birth before labor begins a Zion-mother poem that asks who has heard such a thing, answers with sudden national birth, invites rejoicing and nursing, promises peace and glory, and ends with comfort, flourishing, and a servants-enemies contrast. Fire arrives only at verse 15.
repairs.boss_rationale: Accept 66:7-14 as Zion birth and maternal consolation. Birth, nursing, river, carrying, and mother-comfort imagery develop one poem to the hand-and-indignation hinge; splitting comfort from birth would remove the answer from its governing paradox.

primary_reviews.support: Beterem tahil begins the birth paradox, and the servant/enemy antithesis at verse 14 closes before the ki-hinneh fire arrival.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Pronouns and the relation between city, land, and people remain interpretive questions rather than seam authorities.

primary_reviews.support: Sudden birth, astonished questions, communal rejoicing, maternal feeding, peace-river promise, carrying, comfort, and flourishing create one coherent poem.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The imagery changes several times, but every development elaborates Zion's maternal reversal.

primary_reviews.support: Birth and mother-Zion parallels cannot identify referents or subdivide the poem.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later reuse should not extract a single birth or comfort line from its complete movement.

repairs.defensible_basis: The fire-and-chariot arrival at verse 15 begins judgment and condemned-rite material, but verse 18 is syntactically abrupt: works and thoughts look backward while the gathering of nations looks forward to mission, enduring seed, worship, and the corpse image. The exact 17/18 attachment remains unresolved.
repairs.boss_rationale: Hold 66:15-24 as the book-final parent. Surfacing 15-17 and 18-24 would respect judgment and nations-finale forms, yet correlated Hebrew witnesses cannot settle verse 18's ellipsis; the larger unit prevents a falsely exact seam while preserving both options for external review.

primary_reviews.support: Verse 17 closes condemned rites, but we'anokhi ma'asehem u-mahshevoteyhem at 66:18 lacks an explicit finite transition before the nations-gathering clause.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC represent the same Leningrad-family textual stream and cannot independently settle the elliptical attachment.

challenge.claim: The relation of 66:18 to judgment and gathering is textually and syntactically unresolved.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Obtain direct MT-LXX-DSS textual and Hebrew discourse review before surfacing 66:15-17 and 66:18-24.

primary_reviews.support: Judgment arrival and nations mission are distinct final movements, and verse 18 plausibly launches the latter despite its backward-looking nouns.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The corpse-image ending also recalls judgment, making the finale deliberately interwoven.

challenge.claim: The held parent suppresses two retrievable forms in the book's close.
challenge.proposed_remedy: Test two children under mandatory 66:15-24 hydration once verse 18's literary role is independently adjudicated.

primary_reviews.support: Later mission, new-creation, worship, and judgment relations cannot resolve the grammar at Isaiah 66:18.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical reuse may pull the route toward thematic subdivisions that outrun the local syntax.
